meta.blurb: Ada Brennan has kept house at Fenwick House for thirty years and written down every small thing she noticed. When her employer dies after his birthday dinner, the police look at her first. Her green notebook may be the only proof she has.
meta.bible: Ada Brennan: 58, the housekeeper of Fenwick House for thirty years; keeps a small green Notebook of everything she notices while she cleans; notices small things and writes down the time. Leopold Ashgrove: 80 on the Saturday of the story, a retired shipbuilder and owner of Fenwick House, sharp and kind; weak heart; takes small blue oval Tablets twice a day from a blue Pill box; dies in his library chair on Saturday night. Ivor Spence: his secretary of twelve years, neat and pale, always has a striped bag of white mints from Hobb's shop; secretly sold three rare books to pay gambling debts; swapped the tablets for mints on Friday morning between 7:50 and 8:05; he is the culprit. Mrs Dunmore: the cook of twenty-six years. Joel Reyes: the young nurse who fills the pill box every second Sunday, away at his sister's wedding from Thursday. Clara Ashgrove: Leopold's niece, 34, a schoolteacher, arrived Friday at half past six in the evening. Rupert Ashgrove: his nephew, charming and short of money, arrived Saturday at four o'clock in a sports car. Dr Whitlow: the village doctor. Inspector Joan Pryce: the police detective. Mr Lowell: a book dealer in the city who bought the three books in March from Ivor and did not know they were stolen. Places: Fenwick House, the village of Thistlebeck, Hobb's shop, the Library with its glass Cabinet and brass key. The three missing books are old sea books, bound in brown leather. Facts: Friday 7:50 Leopold takes a blue tablet and leaves the box on the library desk for a telephone call; 8:05 Ada finds the box there with Ivor alone, white dust on his fingers; on Monday Leopold planned a full Count of the books and a new lawyer; his new Will was never signed. Key terms: Housekeeper, Secretary, Notebook, Inspector, Tablets, Mints, Cabinet, Ledger, Timeline, Invoice, Solicitor, Pharmacist, Warrant, Gambling. Voice and tone: calm, observant and warm, a fair-play puzzle told through small details; the death is stated plainly with no gore; the housekeeper's patience solves it.

B1B2: Ada Brennan had kept house at Fenwick House for thirty years, and every morning she wrote in a small green notebook. Today was Saturday, and old Mr Leopold Ashgrove was going to be eighty.
Ada had a habit that she had never lost. While she cleaned, she wrote down small things she noticed, such as a cold cup, an open drawer or a window left unlatched.
Only a few people lived at Fenwick House. There was Mr Ashgrove, his secretary Ivor Spence, the cook Mrs Dunmore and Ada, and a nurse named Joel Reyes who was away this weekend.
Mr Ashgrove sat in the library with his blue pill box on the desk beside him. He had a weak heart, and he took small blue oval tablets every morning and every night.
Ivor Spence, the secretary, was always at his desk in the library. He kept a striped paper bag of white mints beside his papers, and he offered one to Ada.
Ada remembered something from the day before. On Friday at five past eight, she had found the blue pill box on the library desk instead of beside Mr Ashgrove's bed, with Ivor sitting alone nearby.
Clara Ashgrove, Mr Ashgrove's niece, had arrived on Friday evening with a bunch of violets. She was a quiet schoolteacher, and she worried about her uncle's health.
At four o'clock on Saturday, Rupert Ashgrove arrived in a fast red car. He was charming, and he asked Ada in a friendly way whether his uncle had changed his will.
Ada looked at the glass cabinet in the library, where the oldest books were kept. There were three gaps on the top shelf, and her notebook said that they had been there since March.
Mr Ashgrove spoke quietly to Ada in the library. He said that he had asked for a full count of every book on Monday, and that he would see a new lawyer that same day.
In the kitchen, Mrs Dunmore was putting the last decorations on an enormous cake. The whole house was busy, and everything smelled of warm bread and roast meat.
At the birthday dinner, Mr Ashgrove stood up to make a speech. He thanked everyone for coming, and then he said, “Some people in this house have been taking from me.”
Nobody spoke, and Ada watched the faces round the table. Ivor put his hand in his pocket, Rupert laughed too loudly, and Clara looked down at her plate.
At ten o'clock, Ada carried a glass of hot milk to the library as she did every night. Mr Ashgrove was sitting at his desk, and he took his evening tablet from the blue box.
Mr Ashgrove said goodnight to Ada and asked her to lock the garden door. She left the library at ten past ten and thought that he looked very tired.
Ada locked the garden door and checked every window downstairs. At midnight she wrote in her notebook, and nothing seemed wrong except the quiet.
On Sunday morning, Ada brought tea to the library at a quarter past six. Mr Ashgrove sat in his chair with the lamp still on and a book on his knee, but he was not breathing.
Dr Whitlow, the village doctor, came within the hour. He said that Mr Ashgrove's old heart had stopped in the night, and that it seemed a natural death.
Inspector Joan Pryce came to Fenwick House to ask the usual questions. She learned that Ada had been the last to see him, and that Ada was named in his will.
Ada looked into the blue pill box on the library desk. Every compartment held small, round, white tablets, and she remembered that the one Mr Ashgrove had taken had been white.

Ada fetched the bottle of medicine from Mr Ashgrove's bathroom. It held blue oval tablets, which were quite different from the white ones in the box, so Inspector Pryce took the box away to be tested.
A few days later, the test results arrived. The white tablets were not medicine at all, but sugar mints, and someone had swapped them for Mr Ashgrove's real tablets.
Inspector Pryce spoke to Ada alone in the morning room. She said that Ada had carried the milk, held the keys and would receive money from the will, which made her an obvious suspect.
Ada opened her notebook at Friday. At 7:50 Mr Ashgrove had taken a blue tablet and then left the room for a telephone call, and at 8:05 Ivor had been alone with the box.
Inspector Pryce read for a long time. She said that many people could have moved the box, but she was impressed by the notes, and she asked Ada to help her.
Together they made a timeline from the notebook. Rupert had not arrived until four o'clock on Saturday, long after the tablets had been changed, so he could not have done it.
Clara had arrived on Friday evening at half past six, after the tablets had already been changed. She wept for her uncle, and Ada was glad that the notebook proved her innocent.

Mrs Dunmore had been in the kitchen on Friday morning, signing for eggs from the grocer's boy. Joel Reyes had been at his sister's wedding, and photographs proved it, so neither of them had touched the box.
Only Ivor Spence had been alone with the box that morning. However, Inspector Pryce said that being near it was not proof, so she and Ada began to look more closely at the library.
Inspector Pryce questioned Ivor Spence calmly. He said that he had gone to bed at nine on Saturday and that he had never touched Mr Ashgrove's pill box in his life.
Ada opened the glass cabinet with the little brass key. Ivor said that the three missing books had been sent to be repaired in March, and that Mr Ashgrove had agreed.
The library record book said that the three books had been sent for binding. It gave no name for the binder, and every line was in Ivor's own handwriting.
In her notebook, Ada found an entry for the fourteenth of March. It said that Ivor had carried a long flat box to his car and had told her it was for the binder.
Inspector Pryce telephoned every bookbinder in the county, and none of them had the three books. However, a dealer in the city, Mr Lowell, had bought them from Ivor Spence.
The laboratory found that the mints in the box came from Hobb's shop in the village. Ada's notebook showed that only Ivor ever carried them, and that on Friday he had white dust on his fingers.
Ada explained to Inspector Pryce why Ivor might have done it. On Monday, Mr Ashgrove would have counted every book, and then everyone would have known that Ivor had sold some of them.
With a warrant, the police searched Ivor's room. In the pocket of his coat, they found a striped paper bag, and inside it lay twenty-six small blue oval tablets.
A pharmacist checked the blue tablets and said that they were Mr Ashgrove's own heart medicine. The number of tablets was exactly the number that had gone missing from the box.
Inspector Pryce laid every piece of evidence on the table in front of Ivor. She showed the notebook, the mints, the missing books, the dealer's invoice and the blue tablets from his coat.
At last Ivor Spence began to speak. He said that he had owed a great deal of money from gambling, and that he had sold Mr Ashgrove's rare books one by one to pay it back.
Ivor admitted that he had changed the tablets for mints, hoping that Mr Ashgrove would be ill and the count would wait. He knew it was dangerous, and he had done it anyway.
Inspector Pryce arrested Ivor Spence, and two officers led him to the police car. The whole house stood silent in the rain as it drove away.
Inspector Pryce apologised to Ada for having suspected her. She said that the little green notebook had first cleared her name and then caught the thief.
Mr Ashgrove had never signed his new will, so the old one stood. Ada was left a gift, and Clara decided to keep the library open for the whole village.
Rupert told Ada that he had come to the party only to ask his uncle for money. He felt ashamed, and he offered to pay to buy the stolen books back.
Mr Lowell, the dealer, drove to Fenwick House and returned the three old books. He had not known that they were stolen, and he accepted a fair price from Rupert.
The whole village came to Mr Ashgrove's funeral. Ada stood up and read from her green notebook about the many small kindnesses that he had shown to everyone.
Clara asked Ada to stay at Fenwick House and help her to list every book in the library. Ada thought about it for a minute, and then she said yes.
Ada gave Clara a small green notebook of her own. She taught her to notice small things, such as a cold cup or a moved book, and to write them down at once.
One bright morning in spring, Ada sat at her window with a cup of tea. She opened her green notebook and wrote that the house was quiet, and that everything was in its place.
C1C2: Long before the rest of Fenwick House stirred, Ada Brennan sat at her bedroom window with a mug of tea and a small green notebook, writing down the first observations of the day. She had been the housekeeper there for thirty years, and it was Saturday, the day on which the master of the house, Leopold Ashgrove, would celebrate his eightieth birthday with a dinner for his family. The house was already humming with the nervous energy of a great occasion.

Ada had a habit that she had never been able to lose, and it had begun on her first day in service: while she cleaned, she wrote down the small things that she noticed. A cold cup, an open drawer, a window left unlatched, a book moved from one shelf to another, each of them was a tiny sentence in the story of the people who lived there. Over thirty years, the green notebooks had filled a whole shelf, and she had never once been bored.

Only a handful of people lived at Fenwick House, and Ada knew every one of them as she knew the creaks of the staircase. There was Mr Ashgrove himself, his secretary of twelve years, Ivor Spence, the cook, Mrs Dunmore, and a young nurse called Joel Reyes, who tended the old man's heart and who was away at his sister's wedding until Monday. That weekend the family would arrive, and the house would be full.

In the library Leopold Ashgrove sat in his leather armchair with the blue plastic pill box on the desk beside him, an eighty-year-old shipbuilder who had never learned to be idle. He told Ada that his heart was an old engine and that the small blue oval tablets inside the box were the oil that kept it turning, and he tapped the lid with a fond, impatient finger. Joel filled the box every second Sunday, he added, so that the old man need only remember to open it.

Ivor Spence, the secretary, was a neat, pale man who had worked at the same desk in the library for twelve years and had never been known to hurry. Beside his blotter there always lay a striped paper bag of white mints from Hobb's shop in the village, and he offered one to Ada with the faintly ceremonious air of a man presenting a medal. She declined with thanks, but she noted the bag, as she noted everything.

While she dusted, Ada's thoughts returned to the previous morning, when at five past eight she had found the blue pill box lying on the library desk rather than on its usual tray beside Mr Ashgrove's bed. Ivor had been sitting alone at his desk a few feet away, and she had carried the box upstairs herself without thinking more about it, though she had written the time in her notebook. It had seemed a small oddity then, and she saw no reason yet to call it more.

Clara Ashgrove, the old man's niece, had arrived on Friday evening in a worn green coat, carrying a bunch of violets and an expression of quiet concern. She was a schoolteacher of thirty-four who visited Fenwick House more often than anyone else in the family, and she had spent the whole of that evening reading aloud to her uncle in the library. Ada, who liked her, had noted that she asked three times whether he was taking his tablets.

At four o'clock on Saturday afternoon a low sports car came crunching up the gravel drive, and out of it stepped Rupert Ashgrove, the old man's nephew, all teeth and shining shoes. He kissed Ada's cheek, praised her cooking in advance and then, in a tone so casual that it was nearly convincing, asked whether his uncle had said anything lately about his will. Ada answered that she was only the housekeeper and went to find the clean towels, writing the time in her notebook.

In the library, Ada paused before the tall glass cabinet where Mr Ashgrove kept his oldest and rarest books, because three gaps had appeared along its top shelf. Her notebook told her that they had been there since the middle of March, and that the books which once filled them were bound in cracked brown leather and smelt of salt and attics. She had asked no questions, since it was not her place, but she had never stopped noticing.

While the others were dressing for dinner, Leopold Ashgrove drew Ada aside in the library and spoke to her in a voice that was soft but steady. He had ordered a complete count of every book in the room for Monday morning, he told her, and he would meet a new lawyer that afternoon, because he meant to change his will. He pressed a small brass key into her palm, the key to the glass cabinet, and asked her to keep it safe.

In the kitchen, Mrs Dunmore bent over an enormous cake, piping the last curl of icing with the concentration of a surgeon, while the air shimmered with the smells of roast lamb, warm bread and woodsmoke. She had cooked for the Ashgroves for twenty-six years and had never once allowed a guest to leave hungry. Ada passed through with a tray of polished glasses, and her notebook recorded that the cake would be ready at seven.

At the birthday dinner Leopold Ashgrove rose from the head of the table, a white-haired figure in a velvet jacket, and thanked his guests for coming with real warmth. Then his voice changed, and in the sudden hush he declared that someone in the house had been taking from him for a long time, and that on Monday he would know exactly who it was. He sat down to a silence so deep that Ada could hear the candle flames.

Nobody spoke, and Ada, standing at the sideboard with a jug of water, studied the faces round the table as a gardener studies the sky. Ivor's hand slid into his jacket pocket as if to check something there, Rupert let out a laugh that was a little too loud and a little too long, and Clara stared at her plate with her cheeks pink. Mrs Dunmore chose that moment to bring in the cake, and the spell broke.

At ten o'clock Ada carried a glass of hot milk along the corridor to the library, as she had done every night for thirty years. Mr Ashgrove sat at his desk beneath the green lamp, looking tired but content, and as she set the glass down he opened the blue box and swallowed his evening tablet with a sip of water. She noticed, without thinking much of it, that the tablet he took was white.

Mr Ashgrove thanked her for the milk, wished her goodnight and asked her to lock the garden door on her way to bed, as he always did. She left the library at ten past ten, closing the door softly behind her, and in the corridor it struck her that he looked more tired than she had ever seen him. She almost turned back, but the thought was gone before the habit of decades could make her act on it.

Ada locked the garden door, checked each window on the ground floor and put out the last lamps along the corridor, and by midnight she was in her room with the green notebook open on her knees. She wrote down the time of every small event of the evening, and as the great clock in the hall struck twelve, she found nothing in the list that seemed wrong. She turned off the light and slept, and she would later wish she had stayed awake.

On Sunday morning, at a quarter past six, Ada carried the early tea along the corridor and opened the library door with her elbow. Leopold Ashgrove sat in his leather armchair with the green lamp still burning and an open book on his knee, and one glance told her that he would never read another page. She set the tray down very gently, as though she might wake him, and then she went to telephone the doctor.

Dr Whitlow, the village doctor, arrived within the hour, a stout grey-haired man who had known Leopold Ashgrove for forty years and who was visibly grieved. After a careful examination he said that the old man's heart had simply stopped during the night, as everyone had long feared it would, and that there was nothing in the room to suggest anything but a natural death. Nobody in the house contradicted him, and most of them were relieved.

Inspector Joan Pryce arrived mid-morning to make the routine inquiries that follow any death in a large house, a spare, watchful woman with a notebook of her own. She learned within minutes that Ada had been the last person to see Mr Ashgrove alive, that she had carried his hot milk, that she held the keys of the house, and that, according to his existing will, she was to receive twenty thousand pounds. The inspector wrote all this down without any change of expression.

While the others talked in the hall, Ada slipped back into the library and looked into the blue pill box that stood on the desk, and her breath stopped in her throat. Every compartment for the days ahead was filled with small, round, white tablets, and suddenly she remembered that the tablet which Mr Ashgrove had swallowed with his milk the night before had been white as well. His own tablets, the ones she had seen him take for years, were blue and oval.

Ada fetched the brown pharmacy bottle from the shelf in Mr Ashgrove's bathroom and laid it on the desk beside the pill box, where the difference was plain to see. The bottle held small blue ovals, exactly as she had recorded them in her notebook for years, while the box was full of round white pills, and Inspector Pryce, after a long silence, sealed the box in a bag and sent it for analysis. It was a quiet gesture, but it changed the mood of the whole house.

The laboratory's report came three days later and was brief and unmistakable: the white tablets in the box were not medicine at all but ordinary sugar mints. Someone had emptied the compartments of Leopold Ashgrove's heart tablets and filled them with sweets, and a man who relied on his medicine for every beat of his heart had gone without it for days. Inspector Pryce read the report twice, and when she looked up, her expression had altered completely.

Inspector Pryce asked to speak to Ada alone, and in the small morning room she laid out her reasoning with polite and terrible clarity. Ada had carried the milk, held every key in the house, had access to the pill box on the very day it was altered and stood to receive twenty thousand pounds, and a clever investigator could hardly overlook such a list. Ada heard her out without interruption, and then she asked, with perfect calm, whether she might fetch her notebooks.

Ada opened the green notebook at the page for Friday and turned it to face the inspector, tapping the lines with one finger. At ten to eight, she had written, Mr Ashgrove took a blue tablet in the library and left the box on the desk to answer a telephone call in the garden room, and at five past eight she had found the box still on the desk with Mr Spence alone beside it. A thirty-year habit had, quite by accident, produced a witness more reliable than any human memory.

Inspector Pryce read for a very long time, turning the pages with the care of someone handling a map of a hidden country. She observed that any of a dozen people might have touched the box, and that a notebook was not yet a case, but she could not conceal her respect for the precision of what she saw. Then, to Ada's surprise, the inspector closed the book and asked her whether she would help to build a timeline.

Together they spread the notebook pages across the table and built a timeline hour by hour, and soon the shape of the days became clear. The tablets had been missing from the box since Friday, for Mr Ashgrove had taken a mint on Friday night and again on Saturday morning, and Rupert Ashgrove had not set foot in the house until four o'clock on Saturday afternoon. Whatever his faults, and Ada knew he had several, he could not have changed the pills.

Clara Ashgrove had not arrived until half past six on Friday evening, hours after the tablets had been altered, and she wept openly in the garden room when the inspector explained that she was no longer in doubt. She had loved her uncle simply and without calculation, and her grief was of the plain, shaking kind that cannot be feigned. Ada, who had half dreaded the opposite conclusion, took her hand and found that it was cold.

Mrs Dunmore had spent that Friday morning in the kitchen, and a receipt for six dozen eggs, signed by her at five to eight, placed her there without any doubt. Joel Reyes had been away at his sister's wedding since Thursday, and a dozen photographs, one of which showed him dancing at the very hour in question, cleared him just as firmly. That left, as the inspector pointed out gravely, a rather short list.

Only one person remained, Inspector Pryce observed, as she walked slowly along the library shelves with her hands behind her back: Ivor Spence, who had been alone beside the pill box at the critical moment. But a man's proximity to a box was not proof of anything, and she told Ada plainly that she needed a motive, a method and a mistake, and had so far only the beginnings of the first. They would have to look more closely at what Mr Ashgrove had meant by the word taking.

Inspector Pryce questioned Ivor Spence in the morning room, and he answered in the dry, tidy sentences of a man who has rehearsed every word. He had retired to his room at nine on Saturday evening, he said, and had never in twelve years laid a finger on his employer's pill box, which was a medical matter and none of his business. Beside his chair a striped paper bag of mints lay on the arm, and Ada, noticing it, said nothing.

With the brass key that Leopold had pressed into her hand, Ada unlocked the glass cabinet and showed the inspector the three empty places on the top shelf. Ivor, who had followed them in, remarked smoothly that the missing books had been sent away for repair in March, and that Mr Ashgrove had agreed to it in person. He spoke with such easy confidence that for a moment even Ada almost believed him.

The library's record book lay open on the desk, and the inspector ran her finger down a column of neat entries that all said much the same thing: sent for binding, March. No binder was named anywhere, no receipt was pasted in, and every line, from the first to the last, had been written in Ivor Spence's careful hand. Mr Ashgrove's signature, which should have authorised the loan, did not appear on any of them.

Ada turned back through her green notebooks to the middle of March, and there, in her own small hand, she found what she was looking for. On the fourteenth, she had written, Mr Spence carried a long flat box to his car and said it was going to the binder, and he had seemed in a particular hurry, with his collar turned up against a mild day. She had noted it merely because it was odd, and now it was a thread worth pulling.

Inspector Pryce spent the afternoon on the telephone in the hall, calling every bookbinder in the county, and not one of them had ever seen the three missing books. A dealer in the city, however, a Mr Lowell, confirmed after some hesitation that he had bought them in March from a polite gentleman named Spence, and that he held an invoice bearing the man's signature. The inspector put down the receiver slowly, like someone setting down a very full cup.

The laboratory's second report was shorter than the first: the mints in the pill box were a kind sold only at Hobb's shop in the village, and fine white sugar dust lay in every compartment of the box. Ada's notebook, turned to Friday, recorded that Mr Spence had been the only member of the household who ever carried those mints and that his fingertips had been white when she found him by the desk. He had wiped them on a handkerchief, she had written, quickly.

Ada explained the motive to Inspector Pryce in a single steady breath: Mr Ashgrove had ordered a complete count of the library for Monday morning, and that count would have revealed to the whole household that the best of his books had long since disappeared. Ivor, who had been secretly selling them for months, had known he had only until Monday, and an old man whose heart was fragile could always be made ill for a week. The inspector listened, and she was beginning to nod.

Armed with a warrant, Inspector Pryce led two officers into Ivor Spence's bedroom, a bare and orderly room that smelled faintly of peppermint. In the pocket of a winter coat hanging at the back of the wardrobe they found a striped paper bag from Hobb's shop, and inside it, instead of mints, lay twenty-six small blue oval tablets. The inspector counted them twice, and her hands were quite steady.

A pharmacist from the village examined the blue tablets under a lamp and confirmed that they were precisely the heart medicine prescribed for Leopold Ashgrove, stamped with the same tiny number as those in the bottle in his bathroom. The count agreed to the last tablet with the number that should have been in the pill box, and it left no room for doubt or coincidence. Somebody had taken them away, and somebody had kept them.

Inspector Pryce laid out the evidence before Ivor Spence in neat order, like a hand of cards: Ada's notebook with its minute-by-minute record of Friday, the laboratory's findings about the mints, the empty places in the glass cabinet, Mr Lowell's invoice with his signature and the stolen tablets from his coat. Each item, she observed, was explicable alone, but together they made a single sentence that no jury would misread. Ivor said nothing, and the colour slowly left his face.

At last the mask of tidy respectability slipped from Ivor Spence, and he spoke in a thin, tired voice that Ada had never heard from him before. He had been gambling for years in secret, he confessed, and the debts had grown until the only way to pay them was to sell Mr Ashgrove's books, quietly, one by one, from the cabinet that nobody opened. Every sale had been meant to be the last, and he had believed, each time, that nobody would ever count.

Then, in a flat and almost inaudible voice, Ivor admitted what he had done on Friday morning while the old man was on the telephone in the garden room. He had replaced the blue tablets with mints, he said, hoping only that Mr Ashgrove would fall ill and that the count would be postponed, but he had known perfectly well that a weak heart without its medicine could fail. He had told himself that he would put the tablets back before it came to that, and he never had.

Inspector Pryce formally arrested Ivor Spence on the steps of Fenwick House, and two officers led him across the wet gravel to the waiting car while the rain drifted down in a fine grey veil. The whole household stood in the doorway to watch, and nobody spoke, because there was nothing left to say that the rain had not already said. When the car's lights disappeared beyond the gates, Mrs Dunmore began quietly to cry.

Before leaving, Inspector Pryce stopped in the hall and shook Ada's hand, offering the apology that she had not been able to give until the case was closed. She admitted that she had begun by suspecting her, as the facts at first demanded, and that it had been the green notebook itself, so patient and so exact, that had cleared her and then caught the real thief. It was, she said, the best piece of witness evidence she had met in twenty years of policing.

The solicitor, reading aloud in the library, explained that Mr Ashgrove had never signed the new will that he had planned to make on Monday, and that the earlier one therefore stood. Ada was remembered with the generous gift she had been promised, the house and the library passed to Clara and Rupert, and Clara, rising with unexpected firmness, announced that she intended to open the library to the whole village. Even Rupert, to Ada's surprise, applauded.

Rupert found Ada in the hall one evening, his sports-car keys dangling from his fingers, and confessed that he had come to Fenwick House only to beg his uncle for money. He was ashamed, he said, of how readily he had asked about the will before his uncle's body was even cold, and he offered to pay for the stolen books to be bought back from Mr Lowell. It was the first honest sentence Ada had ever heard him speak, and she thanked him for it.

A week later Mr Lowell, the dealer, climbed the steps of Fenwick House with the three old books wrapped in brown paper, looking embarrassed and apologetic. He had not known for a moment that they were stolen, he assured them, since Ivor Spence had presented every paper with a flourish, and he accepted without complaint the fair price that Rupert offered. Clara set the books back in their gaps in the glass cabinet one by one, and the shelf looked whole again.

The whole village crowded into the little stone church for Leopold Ashgrove's funeral, and the yew trees outside were hung with the damp breath of the mourners. Clara asked Ada to say a few words, and Ada, who had never in her life spoken in public, stood and read from her green notebook a long list of small kindnesses that the old man had shown without ever mentioning them. When she sat down, the whole church was weeping quietly.

A few weeks later Clara asked Ada, over a pot of tea in the library, whether she would stay at Fenwick House as its housekeeper and help her to catalogue every book on the shelves for the village. Ada, who had half expected to be sent away with a pension, took a full minute to think, because she did not want to speak before she was certain. Then she said yes, and Clara's face lit up like a lamp.

Ada presented Clara with a small green notebook of her very own and began, one afternoon between the shelves, to teach her the habit of a lifetime. She showed her how to look at a room before one cleans it, how to write down a cold cup, a moved book or an open drawer at the very moment of seeing it, and how little things, patiently gathered, tell the truth that big things hide. Clara wrote it all down, and Ada smiled at the neat, eager handwriting.

On a bright morning in spring, with the windows open and the smell of cut grass drifting up from the lawn, Ada sat at her bedroom window with her tea and opened a fresh green notebook. She wrote the date, noted that the library was open to the village, that Clara was already up and humming among the shelves, and that Mrs Dunmore had burned the toast. Then she added, for the first time in thirty years, a line that was not an observation at all: everything is in its place.
